lessons.look: The pipeline and demand are updated in a declared order. Changing that order changes the operational model.
lessons.change: Change the lead time from two to four days while retaining the reorder threshold. Predict the effect.
lessons.question: You ignore outstanding orders when reordering. Which problem can arise?
options: The arrival rate becomes an exact fact.
Lost sales become negative.
Duplicate orders can accumulate while deliveries are still in transit.
lessons.feedback: Inventory position includes stock already ordered. Ignoring it can repeatedly trigger orders for the same shortage.
hints: Distinguish on-hand stock from inventory position.
Follow an order through the pipeline before placing another.
lessons.limit: The model omits backorders, variable lead times, order capacity and seasonality.
source: Art B. Owen · Monte Carlo theory, methods and examples

lessons.title: A queue remembers earlier arrivals
lessons.short: Compute waiting times using arrival and service timelines.
lessons.goal: Compute waiting times using arrival and service timelines.
explain: A queue’s wait is not just its service duration. A customer may arrive while earlier work still occupies the server. For one first-come-first-served server, service starts at the later of the arrival time and the previous completion.

Each simulation row below is a finite sequence of one hundred customers starting with an empty system. Inter-arrival times and service times are independent exponentials with stated means. The code carries the completion time forward so each wait includes work already ahead.

These finite initially empty traces do not establish a steady-state service guarantee. Near or above capacity, longer horizons can reveal waits a short trace conceals. Report arrival assumptions, starting state, observation boundary and whether unfinished customers are retained.
lessons.predict: Can waiting increase even when the service-time distribution stays unchanged?
lessons.look: Customers within one trace share queue state and are not independent samples. Use independent trace summaries for a run-level uncertainty calculation.
lessons.change: Raise arrival_rate to 1.1, then increase the customer horizon. Explain why a short drained queue is not evidence of stable capacity.
lessons.question: Why are successive waiting times in one queue trace usually dependent?
options: They share the backlog left by earlier customers.
They must all have identical values.
A fixed seed makes every model independent.
lessons.feedback: The queue state links observations over time. Resampling customer waits as independent trials can understate estimator uncertainty.
hints: Track the previous completion time.
Ask what a slow service leaves for the next customer.
lessons.limit: This is a finite single-server model with exponential arrivals and services, not a calibrated staffing recommendation.
source: Art B. Owen · Monte Carlo theory, methods and examples

lessons.title: Failure and repair use up time
lessons.short: Estimate finite-horizon availability while accounting for the full observation window.
lessons.goal: Estimate finite-horizon availability while accounting for the full observation window.
explain: Availability over a finite window is the fraction of that window during which the system is working. A failure probability for an entire mission answers a different question. A repairable system can fail and return to service within the same observation.

The model alternates exponential working and repair periods, starts healthy, and clips each interval at the horizon. That clipping prevents a long final interval from contributing time outside the observed window. Retain both working and down time as a ledger check.

For this simple alternating process, a long-run availability reference is mean uptime divided by mean uptime plus mean repair time. A finite window starting healthy need not equal that limit. Compare longer horizons and state the starting condition before interpreting the average.
lessons.predict: Should a repair that ends after the horizon contribute its entire duration?
lessons.look: The time ledger sums to the horizon in every trial. The finite healthy-start result is not automatically a stationary availability estimate.
lessons.change: Increase the horizon to 1000 and compare against the same long-run reference.
lessons.question: Which definition matches finite-window availability?
options: The probability that no failure ever occurs.
Working time within the window divided by the window length.
The number of repairs without regard to duration.
lessons.feedback: Availability accounts for time in service. Mission survival and repair counts are related but different quantities.
hints: Keep the units of the numerator and denominator visible.
Ask how an early failure followed by quick repair should count.
lessons.limit: The model assumes independent exponential working and repair periods and omits shared failures and maintenance scheduling.
source: Art B. Owen · Monte Carlo theory, methods and examples

lessons.title: Vectorise without changing the question
lessons.short: Replace a loop with array operations and verify the same calculation.
lessons.goal: Replace a loop with array operations and verify the same calculation.
explain: Vectorisation applies an operation to arrays rather than executing a Python loop for each scalar. It can reduce interpreter overhead, but the main requirement is that the numerical procedure still represents the same trials.

Generate the random inputs once, then calculate the outcome using a loop and an array expression. This paired check isolates the implementation of the calculation from differences in random draws. Equal-looking averages from different draws would be a much weaker equivalence check.

Large arrays also consume memory. If a simulation needs more draws than fit comfortably, process chunks and combine counts or stable summaries. Do not change the trial definition at chunk boundaries. Timing claims require actual measurements of the relevant environment; this lesson checks answers and storage rather than inventing a speedup.
lessons.predict: What should be held fixed when comparing a loop and a vector expression for correctness?
lessons.look: All implementations use exactly the same random inputs and trial rule. That is why exact equality is a useful check here.
lessons.change: Add another nonlinear term to all three implementations and retain the equality checks.
lessons.question: Two implementations have similar mean outputs from different random samples. Does that establish equivalence?
options: No; compare their outputs on the same inputs and boundary cases.
Yes; one matching average proves every trial rule.
Only the prettier code can be correct.
lessons.feedback: A matching aggregate can conceal different per-trial behaviour. Shared inputs and specific edge cases give a stronger verification.
hints: Separate random-input variation from implementation differences.
Compare the same trial in both versions.
lessons.limit: Answer equivalence does not establish relative execution speed or suitability for every array size.

lessons.title: Compare options in the same possible world
lessons.short: Use common random numbers to reduce noise in a paired option difference.
lessons.goal: Use common random numbers to reduce noise in a paired option difference.
explain: Common random numbers reuse underlying random inputs when comparing alternatives. When outcomes move together positively, this can reduce the variance of their difference. The useful target is the difference itself, not two separately impressive-looking means.

The example estimates the change from U squared to U cubed. Under uniform U their expectations are one third and one quarter, so the exact difference is minus one twelfth. Shared and separate draws have the same target but different comparison variance.

The benefit depends on coupling the alternatives appropriately. If the outcomes move in opposite directions, sharing draws can increase difference variance. Preserve meaningful correspondence between trials and assess the variance of the actual decision statistic.
lessons.predict: Why can shared random inputs make a difference estimate more precise even if neither marginal estimator improves?
lessons.look: The shared-input comparison removes some common fluctuation from the difference. Pairing does not justify independence between the two option outcomes.
lessons.change: Replace one outcome with 1-U and compare paired and unpaired difference variances.
lessons.question: Which quantity should you inspect when judging common-random-number efficiency?
options: Only the variance of option A.
The variance or MCSE of the option difference being estimated.
Only the number of seeds printed.
lessons.feedback: Variance reduction should be assessed for the actual target statistic. A coupling can help one comparison and hurt another.
hints: Write the estimator whose precision matters.
Include the covariance term in the difference variance.
lessons.limit: This example uses an exact one-dimensional coupling. Operational models require care about which random events are meaningfully shared.
source: Art B. Owen · Monte Carlo theory, methods and examples

lessons.title: Give every part of the domain a turn
lessons.short: Construct a stratified estimator with correct stratum weights.
lessons.goal: Construct a stratified estimator with correct stratum weights.
explain: Stratification divides a sampling domain into known pieces, samples within each piece and combines their estimates with the correct weights. For equal-width intervals under a uniform distribution, each stratum has equal probability weight.

Compare ordinary uniform sampling with one random point from each of n equal intervals. Every replicate has the same evaluation budget. Independent replicates let you estimate the spread of the resulting estimators without pretending the stratified points are ordinary iid uniform draws.

The improvement depends on the integrand and stratification. If strata have unequal probability or receive unequal sample counts, the combination must retain their weights. A raw average of all sampled values can otherwise target the wrong distribution.
lessons.predict: Will one draw in every equal-width interval leave the same gaps as ordinary random draws?
lessons.look: The comparison uses equal evaluations per estimate. Replicate-level spread is the relevant numerical-error evidence here.
lessons.change: Replace U squared with an indicator U>0.973 and inspect how performance changes.
lessons.question: Two strata have probabilities 0.9 and 0.1, but you sample equally many draws in each. How should their mean estimates be combined?
options: With equal weights because the sample counts match.
By keeping only the smaller stratum.
With weights 0.9 and 0.1 for the target distribution.
lessons.feedback: Sampling allocation and target probability are different. The estimator must retain the target stratum weights.
hints: Identify the population weight of each stratum.
Do not confuse deliberate allocation with target probability.
lessons.limit: The example is one-dimensional with equal strata. High-dimensional or poorly chosen strata need separate analysis.
source: Art B. Owen · Monte Carlo theory, methods and examples

lessons.title: Pair opposite draws
lessons.short: Use antithetic variates and check whether their covariance is helpful.
lessons.goal: Use antithetic variates and check whether their covariance is helpful.
explain: Antithetic sampling pairs related draws with the same marginal distribution, often U and 1-U for a uniform input. Average the two function values to form one paired observation. If their covariance is negative, pairing can reduce variance.

For a monotone increasing function, high U produces a high value while 1-U produces a low one. The pair can balance. For other functions, both values can move together and the method may provide little benefit or even hurt.

Assess efficiency with the same number of function evaluations. The paired observations, not their individual members, are the independent units for the standard-error calculation. The example compares repeated estimates rather than applying an iid formula to correlated pair members.
lessons.predict: If f(U) equals f(1-U), does the pair provide the usual negative-covariance benefit?
lessons.look: For this monotone integrand the pairing is useful. The result is conditional on the function, not a universal guarantee for opposite inputs.
lessons.change: Try f(U)=(U-.5) squared in both methods and explain the changed covariance.
lessons.question: What is the independent resampling unit in an antithetic estimator built from independent pairs?
options: The whole paired average.
Each of the two correlated members treated independently.
Only whichever member is smaller.
lessons.feedback: The pair members share a draw. Independent paired averages preserve the dependence used by the estimator.
hints: Find what is independently generated.
Keep the two coupled evaluations together.
lessons.limit: Antithetic pairing can fail to reduce variance for non-monotone functions and does not repair biased input models.
source: Art B. Owen · Monte Carlo theory, methods and examples

lessons.title: Subtract a fluctuation you can explain
lessons.short: Construct a control-variate estimator using a known expectation.
lessons.goal: Construct a control-variate estimator using a known expectation.
explain: A control variate is a related random quantity whose expectation is known. Subtracting a coefficient times its deviation from that expectation leaves the target expectation unchanged, while a useful coefficient can reduce variance.

Estimate exp(U) with U as a control and known E[U]=0.5. The coefficient is fitted using a separate pilot sample, then held fixed for the production sample. This separation keeps the simple unbiasedness argument inspectable conditional on the pilot coefficient.

A poor coefficient can increase variance. A wrong claimed control expectation shifts the target and introduces bias. Always state where the reference expectation comes from and compare precision for the actual controlled estimator. More elaborate same-sample coefficient procedures need their own analysis.
lessons.predict: What happens if you subtract a control whose supposed expectation is wrong?
lessons.look: The known expectation is essential, and the pilot costs evaluations too. Include that cost in a fair efficiency comparison.
lessons.change: Replace .5 with .55 as a deliberately wrong reference and inspect the resulting bias against the exact target.
lessons.question: Which control-variate condition protects the target expectation in this construction?
options: The plot has low variance.
The control expectation is correct and the coefficient is fixed independently of production draws.
The coefficient is always positive.
lessons.feedback: The zero-mean adjustment is what preserves the expectation. A precise-looking estimator with a wrong adjustment can be biased.
hints: Take the expectation of the adjustment term.
Separate pilot fitting from production averaging.
lessons.limit: This uses a separate pilot and an exactly known uniform expectation. Real controls may have approximation or estimation error.
source: Art B. Owen · Monte Carlo theory, methods and examples

lessons.title: Spread points with randomised Sobol sampling
lessons.short: Compare randomised quasi-Monte Carlo estimates using independent scrambles.
lessons.goal: Compare randomised quasi-Monte Carlo estimates using independent scrambles.
explain: Quasi-Monte Carlo points are designed to cover a domain more evenly than ordinary independent random points. A scrambled Sobol sequence introduces randomisation while retaining useful structure. It is a different sampling design, so the ordinary iid point-level error formula is not automatically appropriate.

Use a power-of-two point count with random_base2 to preserve the sequence’s balance properties. Each independent scramble produces one estimate. The spread across those estimates provides evidence about randomisation error for this experiment.

The example integrates a smooth two-dimensional function with known answer. Smoothness, dimension, variable ordering and discontinuities can all affect performance. Better coverage in one illustration does not imply every integrand or tail event will improve. Retain the method, scramble seeds and evaluation budget in the record.
lessons.predict: Should the structured points inside one scramble be treated as iid draws for the ordinary standard-error formula?
lessons.look: The independent units for the displayed comparison are whole randomised estimates. Their count is twenty, not 20 times 1024 iid points.
lessons.change: Replace the smooth integrand with a small-region indicator and compare the replicate spread.
lessons.question: What is a defensible basic error check for this randomised QMC experiment?
options: An iid formula applied blindly to structured points.
A claim that evenly spread points have no error.
Independent scrambles with repeated complete estimates.
lessons.feedback: Independent randomisations expose variation of the estimator while preserving the structured sampling within each replicate.
hints: Locate where independent randomisation enters.
Keep the structured sample together as one replicate.
lessons.limit: Replicate spread estimates randomisation error, not model uncertainty. Few scrambles and rare discontinuous events can still give unstable evidence.

lessons.title: Define what a bad outcome costs
lessons.short: Translate an objective into a loss calculation with interpretable units.
lessons.goal: Translate an objective into a loss calculation with interpretable units.
explain: A simulation produces possible outcomes; a decision also needs an objective. A loss function converts an outcome and action into a consequence measured on a stated scale. It makes trade-offs explicit rather than leaving the choice to whichever summary looks favourable.

For a shop’s one-period stocking decision, shortage and leftover stock have different penalties. The same demand outcome can give a different loss under each stock choice. Those penalties express assumptions about consequences and priorities.

Expected loss averages over the modelled demand distribution. It is not necessarily the right objective for every decision: hard service constraints, risk aversion or consequences not captured in money may matter. Keep the probability model and the preference model separately reviewable.
lessons.predict: Can changing a shortage penalty change the preferred stock level without changing demand?
lessons.look: A preference change can change the decision while every demand draw stays fixed. That is not a contradiction in the simulation.
lessons.change: Use a shortage penalty of 3 instead of 10 and compare the ranking.
lessons.question: What does a penalty of £10 per unmet unit represent?
options: A consequence assumption that needs a decision-context justification.
A probability of demand.
A Monte Carlo standard error.
lessons.feedback: A penalty is part of the objective. It should be justified separately from the distribution used to generate demand.
hints: Separate how often something happens from how much it matters.
Name the unit of the loss.
lessons.limit: The illustrative loss omits reputational effects, substitution and multi-period customer behaviour.
source: Art B. Owen · Monte Carlo theory, methods and examples

lessons.title: Compare feasible options
lessons.short: Evaluate all choices under matched simulated conditions and explicit constraints.
lessons.goal: Evaluate all choices under matched simulated conditions and explicit constraints.
explain: A low expected loss does not automatically make an option feasible. A decision can include a service requirement, a spending limit or a physical bound in addition to an optimisation objective.

Compare stock choices under the same demand draws. Here the requirement is a modelled shortage probability no greater than 0.1. The preferred choice among feasible options is then the one with the lowest expected loss under the stated penalties.

A simulation estimate close to a constraint boundary has numerical uncertainty. Treat feasibility as unresolved when that uncertainty could reverse the decision, and do not turn an estimated probability into a guarantee. Model uncertainty can be larger still, especially when the future demand distribution was assumed.
lessons.predict: Should an option with lower mean loss be accepted if it violates the declared service requirement?
lessons.look: The table explicitly labels the rule as using point estimates. Near a boundary, calculate numerical uncertainty and test input assumptions.
lessons.change: Tighten the service requirement from .1 to .02 and report whether any tested option remains feasible.
lessons.question: No tested option meets the requirement. What should the report say?
options: Declare the cheapest one feasible anyway.
State that none of the tested options meets the requirement under the model, then propose alternatives.
Delete the constraint after looking at results.
lessons.feedback: Infeasibility is a useful result. A new option or revised requirement should be explicit rather than hidden in the analysis.
hints: Apply the declared constraints before ranking feasible options.
Retain evidence when every candidate fails.
lessons.limit: The procedure compares a finite candidate list and uses estimated probabilities. It is not a proof of global optimality or guaranteed service.
source: Art B. Owen · Monte Carlo theory, methods and examples

lessons.title: Inspect the downside as well as the mean
lessons.short: Report tail loss measures with an explicit convention and sampling limitations.
lessons.goal: Report tail loss measures with an explicit convention and sampling limitations.
explain: A mean loss can conceal severe outcomes. A quantile such as P95 marks a boundary in the outcome distribution, while a tail mean averages losses in a selected upper tail. They answer different questions.

For a continuous loss model, averaging values at or above the estimated P95 is a simple empirical upper-tail mean. With discrete outcomes or ties at the threshold, this threshold-based convention need not equal the expected-shortfall definition using exactly the worst 5% of probability mass. State the convention.

Tail estimates use fewer effective observations than central estimates. Retain the number of contributing trials and compare independent runs or justified uncertainty methods. A well-estimated model tail is still conditional on assumptions about extreme outcomes.
lessons.predict: Will a 95th-percentile threshold and the mean beyond it usually have the same value?
lessons.look: The sample maximum can change substantially with trial count. It is not an estimate of a finite absolute worst case for an unbounded model.
lessons.change: Increase the log-scale SD and compare the mean, P95 and tail mean.
lessons.question: Why can a tail mean be unstable even when the overall mean looks stable?
options: Tail estimates always use every value equally.
The histogram colour changes the estimator.
A small number of extreme observations may dominate the tail calculation.
lessons.feedback: Tail quantities depend on relatively few large outcomes. Assess their sample support and numerical uncertainty separately.
hints: Count the observations that contribute to the tail.
Consider what one much larger outcome would do.
lessons.limit: The loss model is invented and unbounded. Real consequence tails and appropriate risk objectives need domain evidence.
source: Art B. Owen · Monte Carlo theory, methods and examples

lessons.title: Find where the decision changes
lessons.short: Use sensitivity scenarios to identify a recommendation’s boundary.
lessons.goal: Use sensitivity scenarios to identify a recommendation’s boundary.
explain: A robust recommendation should explain which assumptions support it and where it changes. Sensitivity analysis deliberately varies an input or relationship while retaining the decision procedure.

Here demand mean is a scenario input. Every scenario compares the same stock options and penalty rule, then reports its preferred choice. The result is a decision map, not a probability distribution over scenarios.

Changing one input at a time can be useful for understanding, but can miss interactions. Once a boundary is visible, test combinations of uncertain assumptions near it. The most valuable next measurement may be an input that determines which side of the decision boundary the real situation lies on.
lessons.predict: If the preferred stock rises with assumed demand, does that mean the scenario rates have been estimated from data?
lessons.look: The input values were chosen for exploration. The table shows conditional decisions, not estimated scenario probabilities.
lessons.change: Repeat the map with a different shortage penalty and look for interactions.
lessons.question: A decision is unchanged over a wide tested range of one input. What does that support?
options: Robustness to that tested variation under the rest of the model, with other uncertainties still open.
Proof that every assumption is correct.
A guarantee of optimality under all possible futures.
lessons.feedback: A sensitivity result has a defined scope. It can support a local robustness claim without validating every part of the model.
hints: Name exactly which input was varied.
Keep untested assumptions visible.
lessons.limit: A finite one-input sensitivity map can miss interactions, discontinuities and plausible conditions outside the tested range.
source: Art B. Owen · Monte Carlo theory, methods and examples

lessons.title: What would better information be worth?
lessons.short: Calculate expected regret and an upper bound from perfect information.
lessons.goal: Calculate expected regret and an upper bound from perfect information.
explain: Regret compares an action’s loss with the best action for the same realised state. Before seeing the state, choose the action with the lowest expected loss. A hypothetical perfect-information decision can choose separately for every state.

The expected value of perfect information is the minimum expected loss before information minus the expected minimum loss with perfect state information. It is nonnegative in the coherent model and provides an upper bound on the value of an imperfect signal before information costs.

This is an upper bound under a specified model and information timing. Real measurements are noisy, delayed or limited to some inputs. Their expected value requires modelling the signal and the decision after observing it; it is not generally equal to the perfect-information bound.
lessons.predict: Can an imperfect forecast be worth more than knowing the full future state for the same decision, before costs?
lessons.look: The perfect-information policy chooses after observing the simulated state. It is a hypothetical bound, not an implementable forecast.
lessons.change: Restrict the candidate stock levels and observe how the information value depends on the available actions.
lessons.question: A noisy survey costs more than the model’s EVPI bound for this decision. What does that suggest?
options: The survey must be perfectly accurate.
It cannot be justified by this modelled decision benefit alone, before considering other benefits or model revisions.
The calculation proves information has no value anywhere.
lessons.feedback: EVPI bounds the benefit for the specified decision and information timing. Other benefits and model adequacy should be stated separately.
hints: Compare information cost with the maximum modelled decision improvement.
Keep the scope of the decision explicit.
lessons.limit: The calculation assumes risk-neutral expected loss, a finite action set and the supplied demand model. It does not estimate the value of a particular real survey.
source: Art B. Owen · Monte Carlo theory, methods and examples

lessons.title: A policy can respond to new information
lessons.short: Compare an adaptive decision with a fixed decision using the information actually available.
lessons.goal: Compare an adaptive decision with a fixed decision using the information actually available.
explain: A policy maps available information to an action. It differs from a fixed choice and from an impossible hindsight rule that sees the future. Specify when the signal arrives and what it reveals before allowing the policy to act.

In this example a noisy early signal is related to later demand through a shared latent condition. A fixed stock is compared with a policy that stocks more after a high signal. Neither policy can inspect realised demand before acting.

Use matched simulated conditions to compare losses. Optimising a threshold on one batch and reporting its apparent performance on that same batch can overfit simulation noise. Hold out independent evaluation trials when selecting a policy from many candidates.
lessons.predict: Would a policy that chooses stock after seeing final demand be a fair operational comparison?
lessons.look: The adaptive rule sees the noisy signal, not final demand. Its usefulness depends on both signal quality and the action rule.
lessons.change: Increase the signal noise SD and evaluate the same fixed threshold policy on fresh draws.
lessons.question: You test a hundred policy thresholds and select the lowest-loss one. What improves the performance assessment?
options: Reporting only its best training-batch result.
Allowing it to inspect future outcomes.
Evaluating the selected policy on an independent simulation batch under the declared model.
lessons.feedback: Independent evaluation helps separate genuine policy performance from selecting a favourable noise realisation.
hints: Separate policy selection from policy evaluation.
Keep the information available at decision time fixed.
lessons.limit: The signal mechanism and policy are invented. Independent simulation evaluation does not establish real-world signal quality.
source: Art B. Owen · Monte Carlo theory, methods and examples

lessons.title: Test a small case you can solve
lessons.short: Verify model arithmetic with boundary cases and independent references.
lessons.goal: Verify model arithmetic with boundary cases and independent references.
explain: Verification asks whether the implementation follows the stated model. A small exact case is often more revealing than a large plausible-looking simulation. Choose inputs that force zero, certain or easily calculated outcomes.

For a stocking-loss function, demand equal to stock should create neither shortage nor waste. Zero demand should leave all stock unused. Demand above stock should incur shortage cost only for the missing units. These cases test signs, boundaries and units without relying on random variation.

Keep reference calculations independent of the implementation being checked. Copying the same expression into an expected-answer cell can preserve the same bug. Once the deterministic rule passes, test its use across random inputs and retain every failed case while investigating.
lessons.predict: Can a plausible simulated mean conceal a sign error in a per-trial loss?
lessons.look: The assertions check specific model properties. They do not establish that the penalty values describe real consequences.
lessons.change: Add a zero-stock case and a fractional-cost case, calculating the references separately.
lessons.question: What does a passing implementation test establish?
options: That the tested code behaviour matches the stated reference cases.
That the model is empirically valid in every domain.
That more real-world data are unnecessary.
lessons.feedback: Verification checks implementation against a specification. Empirical validation asks whether that specification is useful for the real question.
hints: Separate the code rule from the real-world mechanism.
Name exactly what the test compares.
lessons.limit: A finite set of tests can miss untested cases and cannot establish empirical validity.
source: Art B. Owen · Monte Carlo theory, methods and examples

lessons.title: Compare predictions with observations
lessons.short: Use held-out evidence to challenge a model’s predictive behaviour.
lessons.goal: Use held-out evidence to challenge a model’s predictive behaviour.
explain: Validation asks whether a model is adequate for its intended use. It can involve comparing predictions with observations that were not used to choose or fit the model. A model can pass arithmetic checks while failing this empirical comparison.

This illustration supplies an invented held-out demand record and compares it with an assumed Poisson prediction. Count how often observations exceed the model’s nominal 90th percentile. With a small validation set the count is itself variable, and repeated time observations may be dependent.

A discrepancy can reveal a poor model, changed conditions, a measurement problem or a mismatched validation population. It should lead to investigation. Do not delete inconvenient validation observations or retune on them while continuing to call them an untouched test set.
lessons.predict: Does a prediction covering about 90% in its own simulated data guarantee 90% coverage on new observations?
lessons.look: Discrete quantiles can have coverage above the nominal level. The held-out sample is tiny and deliberately illustrative.
lessons.change: Compare another assumed mean without claiming that the holdout remains untouched after model selection.
lessons.question: After repeatedly tuning a model to one validation set, what is needed for a fresh assessment?
options: Only a new random seed for the same fitted model.
New independent evidence or a properly designed resampling/validation strategy.
Renaming the old validation file.
lessons.feedback: Repeated model selection uses information from the validation data. A fresh performance claim needs an evaluation strategy that accounts for selection.
hints: Ask whether the observations influenced the final model.
Separate model revision from evaluation of the revised model.
lessons.limit: The holdout record is invented and too short for a strong calibration claim. Its purpose is to show the validation distinction.

lessons.title: Push the boundaries deliberately
lessons.short: Check invariants, extreme inputs and physical constraints before trusting an estimate.
lessons.goal: Check invariants, extreme inputs and physical constraints before trusting an estimate.
explain: An invariant is a relationship that should hold throughout the calculation, such as a probability lying between zero and one or a stock ledger never creating negative served demand. Extreme inputs can expose errors a typical case does not reach.

Test an inventory allocation rule with zero stock, zero demand and a demand far above stock. Served units must lie between zero and demand. Served plus unmet demand must equal demand. These accounting identities hold independently of any distribution used to generate demand.

Also test whether input units and supports are compatible with the model. An assertion that a sampled number is positive does not justify clipping an inappropriate generator. Stop and revise an invalid input or model rather than quietly transforming evidence until tests pass.
lessons.predict: Which is stronger evidence for a ledger than merely getting a positive average?
lessons.look: The ledger checks every listed trial. A mean can hide both positive and negative errors that cancel.
lessons.change: Introduce an intentional bug such as served=demand, observe the failed check, then restore the correct rule.
lessons.question: A model produces negative durations. What is the useful first response?
options: Silently replace them and report the original model name.
Print fewer decimals.
Investigate whether the input support or calculation is wrong and document any revised model.
lessons.feedback: A physical constraint violation is evidence to investigate. A silent edit changes the model and can hide the cause.
hints: Check whether the invalid result was generated or calculated.
State the revised assumption if you change the model.
lessons.limit: These invariants verify an allocation rule, not the empirical suitability of a demand forecast.
source: Art B. Owen · Monte Carlo theory, methods and examples

lessons.title: Give parallel runs independent streams
lessons.short: Create replayable child random streams without duplicating work.
lessons.goal: Create replayable child random streams without duplicating work.
explain: A seed controls a generator’s initial state. Starting every worker from the same seed repeats the same sequence and does not provide independent simulation batches. Parallel execution needs a deliberate stream design.

NumPy SeedSequence can spawn reproducible child sequences intended for separate generators. Keep each child’s role and the parent seed recorded. Stream design is distinct from operating-system scheduling: this lesson creates the streams sequentially so the numerical behaviour remains inspectable.

When using chunks, avoid resetting a generator to the same state for every chunk. That would repeatedly recycle the same random inputs. Record enough metadata to reproduce the procedure, including package versions, algorithm, draw order and any changes in how workers receive streams.
lessons.predict: What happens if every worker is initialised with exactly the same seed?
lessons.look: The child streams differ while the overall construction can be replayed. Different sample values alone would not prove arbitrary generators independent.
lessons.change: Compare with four generators all created using default_rng(2026). Explain the duplicated batches.
lessons.question: Which record best supports replay of a multi-stream simulation?
options: Parent seed, stream construction, generator/package versions and worker-to-stream mapping.
Only the final average.
A different unrecorded seed on every rerun.
lessons.feedback: A reproducible stream design records the mapping from initial state to simulation work. Final summaries alone do not preserve that procedure.
hints: List what determines each worker’s random inputs.
Keep the assignment rule as well as the seeds.
lessons.limit: The example illustrates stream construction without running actual parallel workers or claiming a parallel speedup.

lessons.title: Write a claim the evidence supports
lessons.short: Attach assumptions, numerical precision and scope to a simulation finding.
lessons.goal: Attach assumptions, numerical precision and scope to a simulation finding.
explain: A useful report identifies the decision, target quantity, model, input evidence, simulation design and result. It keeps numerical uncertainty separate from uncertainty about the model and from variability of individual outcomes.

The example estimates a shortage probability and reports its binomial Monte Carlo interval. That interval is conditional on the assumed demand model. Scenario sensitivity or parameter uncertainty would need additional calculations and should not be implied by the narrow interval.

Write the next discriminating check as part of the finding. If a different demand shape reverses the recommendation, the useful next step may be measuring that shape rather than simulating the current one more precisely. Retain code, inputs and version metadata so another person can inspect the chain from assumptions to conclusion.
lessons.predict: Which uncertainty is quantified by the interval printed below?
lessons.look: The output states the model and denominator. A decision still needs input provenance, consequences and a relevant service requirement.
lessons.change: Write a second finding for an alternative demand scenario and state whether the preferred choice changes.
lessons.question: A narrow MC interval is reported without any input provenance. What remains unresolved?
options: Whether the computation printed a number.
Whether the model and its inputs are credible for the real decision.
The number of colours in the chart.
lessons.feedback: Numerical precision cannot establish the credibility of the modelled world. Retain the evidence and assumptions supporting the inputs.
hints: Separate precision within a model from evidence for that model.
Identify which input the result depends on most.
lessons.limit: The example demonstrates reporting conditional numerical uncertainty, not a validated real stocking recommendation.

lessons.title: Publish your own investigation
lessons.short: Export a reproducible analysis and a scoped decision or uncertainty report.
lessons.goal: Export a reproducible analysis and a scoped decision or uncertainty report.
explain: Choose a general problem: time and budget, demand and resources, or measurement and reliability. Define the question, target quantity, units, input provenance, dependency assumptions, trial budget and validation checks before interpreting the final result.

The editor provides three starter cases. Set case to inventory, project or measurement. Each uses explicitly invented input values unless you upload a CSV containing a positive finite value column. For inventory those values represent demand; for project they represent task durations in days; for measurement they represent radius in centimetres. Uploading validates structure, not provenance, independence or suitability.

Use the report fields to connect the question, model, evidence, result, uncertainty, limitations and next experiment. Export the exact run JSON and a Markdown report alongside your original input file. A finding that leaves a decision unresolved is valid when its assumptions and limits are clear. Independent investigation time is additional to this guided starter.
lessons.predict: Can a structurally valid CSV prove that its values represent the future conditions you care about?
lessons.look: The input label changes when a CSV is used. The simulation count does not increase the amount of observed input evidence.
lessons.change: Choose another starter case or replace the code with your own justified model. Retain a separate plan, validation check and evidence record.
lessons.question: Your modelled decision reverses across two credible input scenarios. What is an honest report?
options: Hide the scenario that gives an inconvenient result.
Use extra decimal places to choose one.
Report the sensitivity, what remains uncertain and a useful next source of evidence.
lessons.feedback: Decision sensitivity is a finding. Identify the evidence that could resolve it rather than confusing more computation with more information.
hints: Separate numerical error from uncertainty about the input world.
State which new observation could change the recommendation.
lessons.limit: The CSV checks do not establish representativeness or independence. The starter models are illustrative and need domain-specific revision before real decisions.
source: Art B. Owen · Monte Carlo theory, methods and examples

lessons.title: Invert a cumulative distribution
lessons.short: Generate a target distribution by transforming a uniform draw through its inverse CDF.
lessons.goal: Generate a target distribution by transforming a uniform draw through its inverse CDF.
explain: A cumulative distribution function, or CDF, gives P(X <= x). Its inverse maps a probability level to the corresponding quantile. Applying that inverse to a uniform draw produces the target distribution under the usual generalised-inverse construction.

For an exponential distribution of mean scale s, the inverse is minus s times log(1-U). NumPy log1p(-U) evaluates log(1-U) accurately when U is small. The generator returns U in [0,1), so this form avoids taking log of zero at the excluded upper endpoint.

The transformation is a sampling mechanism, not evidence that an exponential model fits a real process. Check its support, quantiles and moments against the stated target. Other inverse CDFs may require numerical evaluation, and finite precision can matter in extreme tails.
lessons.predict: What does a uniform probability near one map to in a right-tailed exponential distribution?
lessons.look: The two implementations share the same uniform inputs. The analytical formula and distribution reference agree for these sampled values.
lessons.change: Evaluate the transformation at U=0, .5 and .99 and interpret the units.
lessons.question: What does the inverse CDF take as its input?
options: A probability level between zero and one.
An unscaled duration in days.
An arbitrary negative density height.
lessons.feedback: The inverse CDF maps cumulative probability to a value on the target variable’s scale.
hints: Write the CDF as a map from values to probabilities.
Reverse the direction of that map.
lessons.limit: This example has a closed-form inverse. Other distributions and extreme probabilities can require careful numerical treatment.

lessons.title: Accept or reject a proposal
lessons.short: Construct a rejection sampler using a valid envelope.
lessons.goal: Construct a rejection sampler using a valid envelope.
explain: For a continuous variable, a probability density is a relative height whose integral over a region gives probability. Its height is not the probability of observing one exact continuous value. A rejection sampler proposes from q and accepts with probability p(x)/(M q(x)) when M q bounds the target density p.

Use a uniform proposal on [0,1] for target density p(x)=2x. The bound M=2 makes acceptance probability x. The accepted values should have target mean two thirds, and the acceptance fraction should approach one half.

The envelope bound must hold over the whole contributing support. Choosing M too small makes an acceptance probability above one and invalidates the algorithm. Poorly matched envelopes can also waste most proposals, especially in higher dimensions. Count attempted and accepted proposals separately.
lessons.predict: Will accepted samples remain uniformly distributed when high proposals are accepted more often?
lessons.look: The rejected proposals are part of the computational cost. Only accepted draws belong to the target sample in this construction.
lessons.change: Try target density 3*x squared and derive a valid bound and acceptance probability before editing.
lessons.question: An envelope allows an acceptance probability above one in part of the support. What should you do?
options: Clip it silently and claim the original target.
Correct the envelope or sampler and recheck the target.
Increase the proposal count without changing the bound.
lessons.feedback: A valid dominating envelope is an algorithmic requirement. More samples cannot correct a systematically invalid acceptance rule.
hints: Check the maximum target-to-proposal density ratio.
Ensure every stated acceptance probability lies in [0,1].
lessons.limit: The target is simple and normalised. General rejection samplers need a justified global envelope and may be inefficient.
source: Art B. Owen · Monte Carlo theory, methods and examples

lessons.title: Weight samples from another distribution
lessons.short: Use a target-to-proposal density ratio to estimate a target expectation.
lessons.goal: Use a target-to-proposal density ratio to estimate a target expectation.
explain: Importance sampling estimates an expectation under a target distribution p while drawing from a proposal q. Multiply the function value by p(x)/q(x), then average under q. The density ratio corrects for sampling some regions more or less often.

The target here is standard normal and the function is exp(X). We draw from a normal proposal shifted towards larger X, where the function contributes more. Using the unweighted proposal average would answer a different question.

Work in log densities when convenient, then exponentiate the combined log contribution. The proposal must cover every region where the target integrand contributes, and the weighted estimator needs suitable moments for an ordinary MCSE calculation. A valid estimator can still be so variable that a modest run is misleading.
lessons.predict: Does moving the proposal mean change the target expectation when weights are correct?
lessons.look: The target stays standard normal. The visibly different unweighted average estimates the proposal expectation.
lessons.change: Compare proposal means 0, .5 and 1 using independent batches and the same evaluation budget.
lessons.question: Which ratio corrects a draw from proposal q to target p?
options: q(x)/p(x)
p(x) alone
p(x)/q(x)
lessons.feedback: The correction increases the contribution of regions undersampled by q relative to p and decreases oversampled regions.
hints: Write the expectation as an integral under q.
Insert the ratio that cancels q and restores p.
lessons.limit: The example uses known normal densities and a well-supported target. Weighting does not repair an incorrect target model.
source: Art B. Owen · Monte Carlo theory, methods and examples

lessons.title: A proposal must reach the answer
lessons.short: Detect support mismatch that more importance samples cannot repair.
lessons.goal: Detect support mismatch that more importance samples cannot repair.
explain: A proposal needs positive density wherever the target integrand contributes. If it never samples a relevant region, no weight assigned to the samples it does produce can recover that missing contribution.

The target below is uniform on [0,1] and the integrand is X squared. A proposal restricted to [0,.5] omits much of the integral. Its apparent weighted result converges to the contribution from that restricted interval, not the full target expectation.

A mixture proposal can retain broad coverage while concentrating additional samples in a selected region. Its weight uses the full mixture density, not merely the density of the component that happened to generate a particular draw. Correct support is necessary, but a tiny proposal density in an important region can still produce unstable weights.
lessons.predict: Can a million samples restricted to the lower half of the domain reveal the upper half’s contribution?
lessons.look: The restricted result is precisely estimating the wrong domain contribution. The mixture’s full density accounts for both routes to a draw.
lessons.change: Reduce the uniform mixture weight from .2 to .02 and update the density consistently. Inspect variability across runs.
lessons.question: In a mixture proposal, which density belongs in the weight?
options: The complete proposal mixture density evaluated at the sampled point.
Only the density of the selected component.
Whichever component gives the smallest weight.
lessons.feedback: The marginal proposal density describes how the overall algorithm samples each point. Weighting by a different density generally changes the estimator.
hints: Account for every component capable of generating the point.
Write the proposal as a weighted sum of component densities.
lessons.limit: Full support alone does not guarantee finite variance or adequate overlap in a finite run.
source: Art B. Owen · Monte Carlo theory, methods and examples

lessons.title: Keep weights stable on a log scale
lessons.short: Normalise extreme log weights without numerical underflow.
lessons.goal: Normalise extreme log weights without numerical underflow.
explain: Probability densities and likelihood products can be extremely small or large. Direct exponentiation can underflow to zero or overflow to infinity before an otherwise meaningful ratio is calculated.

For log weights l_i, subtract logsumexp(l) before exponentiating to obtain normalised weights. Adding a common constant to every log weight leaves those normalised weights unchanged. The operation stabilises the arithmetic; it does not improve the statistical overlap of target and proposal.

Normalising weights also has a statistical meaning. If a target normalising constant is unknown, using a ratio of weighted sums creates a self-normalised estimator, discussed later. Do not silently replace an ordinary unbiased importance estimator with a different ratio estimator while keeping the original error interpretation.
lessons.predict: Should adding the same constant to every log weight change their normalised proportions?
lessons.look: The stable calculation recovers meaningful relative weights even though direct exponentials all become zero.
lessons.change: Use log weights [-1000,-1000,-1000] and predict the normalised result.
lessons.question: Does stable log arithmetic ensure that importance sampling has explored every important region?
options: Yes; arithmetic stability proves statistical validity.
No; numerical stability and sampling overlap are separate checks.
Only if weights sum to one.
lessons.feedback: Log arithmetic prevents some floating-point failures. It cannot create samples from a missed region or establish a suitable proposal.
hints: Separate the values stored in memory from the states visited.
Ask whether a stabilised weight can represent a state never sampled.
lessons.limit: The demonstration concerns floating-point arithmetic on supplied weights, not validation of an underlying probability model.

lessons.title: See a rare event more often
lessons.short: Estimate a rare normal-tail probability with a shifted proposal and correct weights.
lessons.goal: Estimate a rare normal-tail probability with a shifted proposal and correct weights.
explain: Naive Monte Carlo can miss an event whose probability is far smaller than one divided by the trial budget. A zero event count then provides little relative precision. Importance sampling can deliberately visit the rare region more often while correcting the changed sampling distribution.

For a standard normal tail above five, draw instead from a normal distribution centred at five. The event now occurs often under the proposal. Multiply its indicator by the target-to-proposal ratio to estimate the original target probability.

The proposal hit rate is not the target event probability. Report weighted contributions and their MCSE, the proposal definition and an exact reference where available. For other rare events, a poor proposal can give unstable or misleading estimates despite many apparent hits.
lessons.predict: If half the shifted-proposal draws exceed five, is the standard-normal tail probability one half?
lessons.look: The weighted estimate returns to the original target scale. The shifted proposal’s frequent hits only make that target easier to estimate.
lessons.change: Compare shifts of 3, 5 and 7 across independent runs. Use weighted MCSE and reference error, not hit count alone.
lessons.question: Which number estimates the original rare-event probability?
options: The proposal fraction in the event.
The number of accepted samples alone.
The average target-weighted event contribution.
lessons.feedback: The importance weights correct for deliberately oversampling the rare region. Omitting them changes the target.
hints: Write the target and proposal separately.
Apply the density correction before averaging the indicator.
lessons.limit: The normal-tail reference is exact for this model. Rare-event validity in an operational model still depends on its structure and input evidence.
source: Art B. Owen · Monte Carlo theory, methods and examples

lessons.title: When one weight dominates
lessons.short: Use weight concentration as a diagnostic without treating it as a precision guarantee.
lessons.goal: Use weight concentration as a diagnostic without treating it as a precision guarantee.
explain: Normalised importance weights reveal how much a finite weighted sample relies on a few observations. A common weight effective-sample-size diagnostic is one divided by the sum of squared normalised weights. Equal weights give the raw count; a single dominant weight gives about one.

This weight ESS is not a universal sample count for every function. It differs from autocorrelation-based MCMC ESS and cannot detect every missing region. A proposal may entirely miss an important mode while the observed weights look innocuous.

Compare shifted normal proposals for a standard normal target. A larger shift creates poorer overlap for this target, and a few rare low values can dominate the weighted approximation. Repeat the experiment and inspect the target quantity, weight distribution and known references rather than trusting one diagnostic number.
lessons.predict: Does a large weight ESS prove that no important target region was missed?
lessons.look: The displayed weighted mean is self-normalised. Its finite-sample bias and variability remain relevant even if the arithmetic is stable.
lessons.change: Increase the shift to 6 in a separate run and inspect instability across seeds.
lessons.question: What does weight ESS mainly summarise in this calculation?
options: Concentration of the observed normalised weights.
A proof of target coverage.
The exact numerical error of every possible weighted statistic.
lessons.feedback: Weight ESS diagnoses concentration in the sample you have. It is a useful warning, not a guarantee of overlap or estimator precision.
hints: Read the formula 1/sum(w²).
Consider a target region from which you obtained no samples.
lessons.limit: Weight ESS is a heuristic diagnostic and does not replace support, overlap, moment and target-specific error checks.
source: Art B. Owen · Monte Carlo theory, methods and examples

lessons.title: An unknown normalising constant
lessons.short: Construct a self-normalised importance estimate and recognise finite-sample ratio bias.
lessons.goal: Construct a self-normalised importance estimate and recognise finite-sample ratio bias.
explain: Sometimes a target density is known only up to a positive multiplicative constant. Dividing weighted function sums by weighted mass sums cancels that constant. This is self-normalised importance sampling.

The estimator is a ratio of random quantities. Even when numerator and denominator individually have suitable expectations, the expected ratio is not generally the ratio of expectations. Self-normalised estimates are typically biased at finite sample sizes, while remaining consistent under appropriate conditions.

The target below has unnormalised density exp(-x to the fourth divided by four). Its symmetry and an analytical second moment give useful checks. A normal proposal covers the support. Stable normalised weights produce an estimate of E[X squared], not an unbiased ordinary-importance integral with a known normaliser.
lessons.predict: Does cancelling an unknown constant also eliminate every finite-sample bias?
lessons.look: The analytical check is valuable because a stable-looking ratio can still be inaccurate. Ordinary iid SE of the raw X squared values would ignore the weights and ratio.
lessons.change: Compare independent repetitions at n=100, 1000 and 20000. Keep finite-sample variability separate from a theoretical bias claim.
lessons.question: Which statement fits a self-normalised importance estimator?
options: It is always exactly unbiased at finite n.
It can be consistent under assumptions while retaining finite-sample ratio bias.
It never needs proposal support checks.
lessons.feedback: Normalising can remove an unknown constant but changes the estimator into a ratio. Its convergence and error analysis need the appropriate assumptions.
hints: Compare E[A/B] with E[A]/E[B].
Check support and overlap even when constants cancel.
lessons.limit: This uses a tractable one-dimensional target. General self-normalised error estimation and multi-modal overlap require further checks.
source: Art B. Owen · Monte Carlo theory, methods and examples

lessons.title: Update a probability with evidence
lessons.short: Combine a beta prior with a binomial likelihood to obtain a posterior.
lessons.goal: Combine a beta prior with a binomial likelihood to obtain a posterior.
explain: Bayesian inference represents an uncertain parameter with a distribution. A prior describes the parameter before the selected observations. A likelihood describes how observations vary for a given parameter. Their product, normalised to integrate to one, is the posterior.

For independent yes/no observations with one common probability p, the binomial likelihood is proportional to p to the successes times (1-p) to the failures. A beta prior has density proportional to p to the (a-1) times (1-p) to the (b-1), for p between zero and one. Multiplication therefore gives a beta posterior with updated shape parameters.

The invented observation is 18 successes in 30 trials, with a beta(2,2) prior. This calculation is exact and does not need Monte Carlo. Establishing the target first gives the later sampling algorithms something known to check. The prior and observation model are assumptions that deserve inspection, especially with limited data.
lessons.predict: Will 18 successes out of 30 make the posterior mean exactly 18/30 under this prior?
lessons.look: The posterior interval concerns the uncertain probability p conditional on this prior, data and likelihood. It is not a range of counts in the next group.
lessons.change: Change the prior to beta(20,20). Describe how much the same observations move its mean.
lessons.question: A stronger prior concentrates near 0.5. What should you examine before using it?
options: Only whether the random seed is fixed.
Whether that concentration is justified and how sensitive the posterior is to it.
Whether the posterior has exactly the sample proportion as its mean.
lessons.feedback: The prior contributes information. Make its concentration and sensitivity explicit instead of treating it as a purely numerical setting.
hints: Compare prior concentration with the amount of observed evidence.
Recalculate under plausible alternative priors.
lessons.limit: A common fixed p and independent observations are assumed. This toy update does not address clustering, selection or changing probabilities.

lessons.title: Sample a posterior directly
lessons.short: Use independent posterior draws to estimate a posterior probability with a numerical error check.
lessons.goal: Use independent posterior draws to estimate a posterior probability with a numerical error check.
explain: Once a posterior distribution is available, Monte Carlo can estimate a probability or expectation under it. Direct beta draws are independent in this example, so the ordinary independent-sample standard error applies to their average or event indicator.

The question is P(p above 0.6 given the invented observations and prior), not the probability of more than 60 percent successes in a future group. Each draw is one possible parameter value under the posterior. Averaging its threshold indicator estimates the posterior probability of that event.

SciPy supplies an exact beta survival function for comparison. This benchmark separates numerical approximation error from posterior uncertainty about p. Raising the draw count improves numerical precision; it does not add observations or narrow the exact posterior distribution.
lessons.predict: Does increasing posterior draws from 1,000 to 100,000 supply more observed evidence?
lessons.look: The posterior SD describes uncertainty in p. MCSE describes numerical error in the estimated posterior event probability. Their units and targets differ.
lessons.change: Estimate P(p > .7), then compare with stats.beta.sf(.7,a,b).
lessons.question: A posterior mean estimate becomes numerically very precise. What follows?
options: The underlying parameter is now known exactly.
The simulation approximates that posterior mean accurately, conditional on the model and evidence.
The prior was necessarily correct.
lessons.feedback: Numerical precision concerns the calculation. The posterior can remain broad and the model can remain uncertain.
hints: Separate the distribution being sampled from its numerical approximation.
Inspect the posterior SD as well as MCSE.
lessons.limit: Independent beta sampling is a convenient benchmark. Correlated Markov-chain draws need different numerical error diagnostics.

lessons.title: Build a Metropolis chain
lessons.short: Implement symmetric-proposal Metropolis while retaining rejected states.
lessons.goal: Implement symmetric-proposal Metropolis while retaining rejected states.
explain: A Markov chain generates its next state from its current state. Metropolis proposes a move and accepts it with a probability constructed to preserve a target distribution. For a symmetric proposal, the acceptance ratio is the target density at the proposal divided by that at the current state, capped at one.

Use log densities to avoid dividing tiny numbers. The beta normalising constant cancels in the ratio. A normal random-walk proposal can land outside the interval zero to one; those proposals have zero target density and are rejected. Clipping them to a boundary would change the proposal and the intended algorithm.

A rejection means the next state equals the current state. Keep that repeated value in the chain: discarding rejections changes the distribution of recorded states. The initial section is warm-up, which we set aside before estimating a mean. This fixed choice is a teaching convention, not proof of convergence.
lessons.predict: Should a rejected proposal disappear from the recorded chain?
lessons.look: The trace is a diagnostic view, not a convergence certificate. Repeated states are an essential part of the sampler.
lessons.change: Compare proposal scales .005 and .8. Observe movement as well as the acceptance fraction.
lessons.question: A tiny proposal has a high acceptance fraction but hardly moves. What does this suggest?
options: High acceptance alone does not establish efficient exploration.
All accepted values are independent.
The posterior must be very narrow.
lessons.feedback: Small steps can produce strong serial dependence. Assess exploration and numerical error rather than maximising acceptance alone.
hints: Look at distance moved per iteration.
A long sequence of nearby states may provide little new information.
lessons.limit: One chain and one trace cannot rule out nonconvergence. This unimodal benchmark is intentionally easier than many posterior targets.
source: Art B. Owen · Monte Carlo theory, methods and examples

lessons.title: Correct an asymmetric proposal
lessons.short: Include the reverse-to-forward proposal ratio in Metropolis–Hastings.
lessons.goal: Include the reverse-to-forward proposal ratio in Metropolis–Hastings.
explain: A symmetric random walk makes forward and reverse proposal densities equal. Other proposals require an additional correction. Metropolis–Hastings accepts using the target ratio multiplied by the reverse proposal density divided by the forward proposal density, capped at one.

An independence proposal draws from a fixed distribution q regardless of the current state. The forward density is q(proposal) and the reverse density is q(current). Although the draw is independent of the current state, these two densities need not be equal. Ignoring their ratio generally changes the stationary distribution.

Here q is beta(3,3), and the target remains beta(20,14). The chain still records rejections and sets aside a starting segment. Comparing with the known mean is a useful implementation check, but one matching mean cannot validate an entire sampler or prove exploration.
lessons.predict: Does drawing an independence proposal make the proposal-density correction unnecessary?
lessons.look: The proposal correction uses current over proposed density for an independence sampler. Reversing that ratio implements a different algorithm.
lessons.change: Change the proposal to beta(10,10) in both the draw and log_q. Inspect acceptance and multiple seeds.
lessons.question: For q(y|x), what proposal factor belongs in the acceptance ratio?
options: q(y|x) / q(x|y).
q(x|y) / q(y|x).
No proposal factor for any algorithm.
lessons.feedback: The reverse-to-forward factor balances the proposed probability flows when forward and reverse moves have different proposal densities.
hints: Identify the proposed forward move x to y.
The correction is reverse density divided by forward density.
lessons.limit: Support and irreducibility still matter. A density ratio cannot rescue a proposal that never reaches relevant target regions.
source: Art B. Owen · Monte Carlo theory, methods and examples

lessons.title: Update one conditional at a time
lessons.short: Implement a Gibbs sampler using the latest value of each coordinate.
lessons.goal: Implement a Gibbs sampler using the latest value of each coordinate.
explain: Gibbs sampling updates components by drawing from their conditional distributions given the other components. Exact conditional draws require no Metropolis rejection step. The resulting sequence is still a Markov chain and its successive states are usually dependent.

For a zero-mean bivariate normal with unit marginal variances and correlation rho, X given Y=y is normal with mean rho*y and variance 1-rho squared. The conditional for Y is analogous. First update X from the current Y, then update Y from the newly drawn X.

The code records a state after both coordinate updates, called a sweep here. Strong correlation can slow movement along a narrow joint distribution even though every conditional draw is accepted. The known means and covariance supply checks; they do not make correlated draws independent.
lessons.predict: In the second update of a sweep, should Y condition on the old X or the newly drawn X?
lessons.look: Conditioning uses the latest state. The lag correlation warns against treating the kept row count as an independent sample count.
lessons.change: Increase rho to .98. Keep enough iterations to inspect the much slower movement.
lessons.question: Every Gibbs update is accepted. What can still make the sampler inefficient?
options: Serial dependence caused by the target geometry.
An obligatory acceptance correction for these exact conditional draws.
The absence of a random seed.
lessons.feedback: Acceptance is not the same as independent information. Strong conditional dependence can make exploration slow.
hints: Inspect the lag correlation.
Compare how quickly coordinates move across the full target range.
lessons.limit: These exact normal conditionals are tractable. More complex targets may need other conditional samplers and stronger diagnostics.
source: Art B. Owen · Monte Carlo theory, methods and examples

lessons.title: Account for serial dependence
lessons.short: Estimate a mean-specific effective sample size rather than using the independent-draw SE.
lessons.goal: Estimate a mean-specific effective sample size rather than using the independent-draw SE.
explain: Autocorrelation describes dependence between a sequence and a lagged version of itself. For a stationary sequence with appropriate finite moments and summable dependence, the variance of its mean includes contributions from all those lag correlations. The independent-draw standard error omits them.

Effective sample size for a particular mean expresses this variance in independent-draw equivalents. It depends on the statistic: the mean of a parameter, its square and a tail indicator can have different effective sizes. An estimate based on one chain can also be unstable.

Use a stationary normal autoregression as a controlled teaching sequence, not a posterior sampler. Its next value equals rho times the previous value plus fresh noise with SD sqrt(1-rho squared). The code estimates autocorrelations by FFT and truncates paired positive lag sums. This simplified routine is for inspecting mean error, not a replacement for modern multi-chain diagnostics.
lessons.predict: For positively correlated draws, will the iid formula usually overstate or understate mean precision?
lessons.look: The known AR(1) approximation gives a reference for this experiment. ESS is not a guarantee that an arbitrary MCMC chain reached its target.
lessons.change: Compare rho=.3 and rho=.95. Repeat with independent seeds and inspect ESS variability.
lessons.question: Can a large ESS for the parameter mean guarantee an accurate rare-tail probability?
options: Yes, all statistics share one ESS.
No; dependence and error are statistic-specific, and target exploration also matters.
Yes, if the chain has more than 1000 rows.
lessons.feedback: Different functions of a chain have different dependence. Tail accuracy requires its own assessment alongside convergence checks.
hints: Replace the parameter by a threshold indicator.
Ask whether that new series has the same autocorrelation.
lessons.limit: The simplified single-chain ESS assumes stationarity and suitable moments. It does not diagnose warm-up, missed modes or tail ESS.
source: Vehtari et al. · Improved R-hat and MCMC diagnostics

lessons.title: Compare multiple chains
lessons.short: Compute rank-normalised and folded split R-hat and explain its diagnostic limits.
lessons.goal: Compute rank-normalised and folded split R-hat and explain its diagnostic limits.
explain: Multiple chains from dispersed starting points can expose disagreement that one trace misses. Split R-hat compares within-chain variation with between-chain variation after splitting each chain in half. Values near one suggest agreement for the features examined, not proof of convergence or target coverage.

Modern diagnostics rank-normalise the pooled split draws to improve robustness, and also examine folded deviations from the pooled median to reveal scale differences. The reported diagnostic is the larger of these two R-hat values. The code implements those steps on two controlled collections of draws.

One collection consists of independent standard normal draws; in the other, one chain has twice the scale. These are constructed diagnostic examples, not actual posterior chains. A practical workflow combines dispersed-chain agreement, bulk and tail ESS, trace and energy/geometry diagnostics where applicable, and checks against the model. No universal threshold certifies every target.
lessons.predict: Could chains have similar means yet disagree about the distribution’s scale?
lessons.look: The folded comparison exposes the deliberately changed scale. Neither collection demonstrates real MCMC exploration of a difficult posterior.
lessons.change: Shift one chain by 1 instead of changing its scale. Compare both diagnostics.
lessons.question: Four chains remain trapped in the same local mode and agree closely. What can R-hat establish?
options: That every mode has been explored.
Agreement among the sampled chains for the diagnostic, leaving missed-mode concerns unresolved.
That all draws are independent.
lessons.feedback: Agreement cannot reveal a region that none of the chains visited. Starting points, model knowledge and complementary diagnostics remain essential.
hints: Consider a second mode absent from every sample.
A comparison only has access to observed chains.
lessons.limit: This implements the rank/folded R-hat calculation, not the full modern MCMC diagnostic suite. Close-to-one R-hat is necessary evidence of agreement, not sufficient evidence of correct inference.
source: Vehtari et al. · Improved R-hat and MCMC diagnostics

lessons.title: Predict new observations
lessons.short: Propagate posterior parameter uncertainty into a future outcome distribution.
lessons.goal: Propagate posterior parameter uncertainty into a future outcome distribution.
explain: Posterior predictive sampling first draws a parameter from its posterior, then draws new observations conditional on that parameter. The resulting distribution accounts for parameter uncertainty and future outcome variability under the model. It is distinct from the posterior distribution of the parameter alone.

For the beta-binomial example, draw p from beta(20,14), then generate a future count among 20 observations with that p. Plugging the posterior mean directly into a binomial omits uncertainty in p. Both have the same expected count here, but the predictive mixture has greater variance.

The beta-binomial distribution gives an exact predictive mean and variance to check this simulation. Predictive checks compare features of replicated data with the observed data to reveal model mismatch. They are model criticism tools, not automatic proof that a prior or likelihood is correct, and a posterior predictive tail comparison is not automatically a calibrated frequentist p-value.
lessons.predict: Can the plug-in and full predictive distributions share a mean but have different spreads?
lessons.look: Count quantiles describe future group outcomes; p quantiles describe a parameter. Neither is the numerical error bar on an estimated mean.
lessons.change: Increase future_n to 100. Compare how parameter uncertainty contributes to the two predictive variances.
lessons.question: Which simulation represents the full posterior predictive count?
options: Fix p at its posterior mean in every draw.
Draw p from the posterior, then draw the new count conditional on that p.
Use the posterior p draw itself as the future count.
lessons.feedback: Two stages propagate both sources of variation under the model. Preserve the distinction between a parameter and an observable count.
hints: Write the units of p and of the count.
First sample the uncertain parameter, then the conditional observation.
lessons.limit: The model assumes future observations share the same p and sampling mechanism as the invented evidence. Changing conditions and model uncertainty require further analysis.

applications.title: Sizing and total cost
applications.short: Compare capacity choices and five-year cost under shared uncertain demand.
applications.goal: Compare capacity choices and five-year cost under shared uncertain demand.
explain: Sizing is a decision about a policy under demand uncertainty. Distinguish useful work, measured sustainable capacity, reserve margin and discrete purchase counts before calculating a price. This optional workbook uses invented capacities and prices to demonstrate a model, not recommend a supplier.

Each world contains an initial daily demand, one annual growth rate and an energy price. All options see those same inputs. A fixed fleet is selected now and held for five years; unmet capacity is reported rather than silently buying extra machines mid-trial. Capital and electricity are the stated cost boundary.

Report both capacity failure probability and a cost distribution. A low expected cost can be unattractive when it fails the demand requirement. More simulation trials refine these conditional summaries; they do not verify benchmark capacity, future growth or purchasing assumptions. Extend the boundary explicitly when adding staffing, support, depreciation or replacements.
applications.predict: Should a cheaper option with insufficient capacity appear feasible merely because its mean cost is low?
applications.look: The required-unit diagnostic describes demand; it does not change the fixed fleet policy or its cost. Costs are nominal undiscounted five-year totals.
applications.change: Add a stated annual support cost per installed unit, and include it consistently for every option.
applications.question: Which comparison is meaningful before choosing a fleet?
options: Only the cheapest single simulated world.
Cost distributions together with a stated capacity reliability requirement and cost boundary.
Capital cost divided by the largest generated demand.
